title: κ λ μ ν π τ φ ζ sound much as in English
body: κ, λ, μ, ν, π, τ, φ, ζ are “k, l, m, n, p, t, f, z”. Say π, τ, κ without the puff of air English adds. Before e and i sounds κ is nearer “ky”.

title: The accent mark shows the stress
body: Every Greek word with more than one syllable carries an accent mark (΄) on the vowel you stress. Moving the stress can change the word, so always follow the mark.

title: α sounds like “a” in “father”, but short
body: α is always an open “a”, as in “father” but kept short. It never turns into the “a” of “cat” or “late”, stressed or not. Only αι and αυ are different (see their rules).

title: ι, η and υ all sound “ee”
body: Three letters share one sound: ι, η and υ are all “ee” as in “see”, but short. υ is never “u” or “y” on its own; it only changes in the pairs ου, αυ, ευ.

title: ο and ω both sound “o”
body: ο and ω are the same sound: a short, pure “o”, between “o” in “hot” and “aw” in “law”. Never glide it into “oh-oo” as in English “go”.

title: ε sounds like “e” in “bet”
body: ε is a short, clear “e” as in “bet”, also at the end of a word, where it is never silent. In the respellings “e” always means this sound.

title: σ and final ς both sound “s”
body: Sigma has two shapes: ς at the end of a word, σ everywhere else. Both are a sharp “s” as in “see”, never the “z” of “rose” (except before soft consonants, see the next rule).

title: ρ is a quick tapped “r”
body: ρ is a light flick of the tongue tip, like the “tt” in American “better”, or rolled a little. Always pronounce it, also before consonants and at the end of a word.

title: ει, οι and υι also sound “ee”
body: These pairs are one vowel, the same “ee” as ι. υι is rare (υιοθεσία “adoption”). Only an accent on the first letter or a diaeresis (οϊ) splits them.

title: Unstressed i sound before a vowel becomes “y”
body: An unstressed ι, ει, οι, η or υ before another vowel glides into a quick “y” and joins that vowel: ιά is “ya”. After λ and ν this gives “ly” as in “million” and “ny” as in “canyon”.

title: ου sounds “oo”
body: The pair ου is one vowel, “oo” as in “food”, but short. It is the only way Greek writes this sound.

title: δ sounds like “th” in “this”
body: δ is always the soft, buzzing “th” of “this” and “mother”, never “d”. Written “dh” in the respellings. Greek writes “d” as ντ.

title: αι sounds like ε, “e” in “bet”
body: The pair αι is one vowel, the same “e” as ε. If the accent sits on the ι (αί) it is still one “e”; only ά before ι or a diaeresis (αϊ) splits it.

title: χ is a rough “kh”, softer before e and i sounds
body: Before α, ο, ω, ου and consonants, χ is the rough “kh” of Scottish “loch”. Before e and i sounds it moves forward to a hiss like the “h” in “huge”, written “h” in the respellings.

title: γ before e and i sounds is “y” as in “yes”
body: Before ε, αι, ι, η, υ, ει, οι, γ sounds like “y” in “yes”. In γι before another vowel the ι is not heard: γιατί is “ya-TEE”.

title: θ sounds like “th” in “thin”
body: θ is always the hard, breathy “th” of “thin” and “bath”, never the “th” of “this” (that one is δ).

title: β sounds “v”, never “b”
body: β is always “v” as in “very”. Greek writes the “b” sound with μπ instead (see that rule).

title: γ is a soft, breathy “gh” before a, o, u sounds
body: Before α, ο, ω, ου and consonants, γ is a “g” said without closing the throat: air keeps flowing, giving a soft gargling “gh”. Written “gh” in the respellings.

title: Final ν joins a following π, τ, κ as “mb”, “nd”, “ng”
body: When a word ending in ν (τον, την, δεν, στον, έναν) is followed by π, τ or κ, they blend like μπ, ντ, γκ inside a word: “mb”, “nd”, “ng”. Say the two words as one.

title: ξ sounds “ks”, ψ sounds “ps”
body: Each is one letter for two sounds: ξ is “ks” as in “box”, ψ is “ps” as in “lips”. Both work at the start of a word too.

title: Double consonants sound single
body: Two identical consonants (σσ, λλ, ββ, νν, μμ…) are said as one, not held longer. Only γγ is different (see its rule).

title: ντ sounds “d” (often “nd” inside a word)
body: At the start of a word ντ is a plain “d”. Inside a word it is usually “nd”, as in “window”, or just “d”.

title: αυ, ευ sound “av”, “ev” before vowels and soft consonants
body: Before a vowel or one of β γ δ ζ λ μ ν ρ, the υ of αυ and ευ turns into a “v”: “av”, “ev”. The accent on αύ, εύ falls on the “a” or “e”.

title: αυ, ευ sound “af”, “ef” before hard consonants
body: Before θ κ ξ π σ τ φ χ ψ and at the end of a word, the υ of αυ and ευ becomes an “f”: “af”, “ef”.

title: μπ sounds “b” (often “mb” inside a word)
body: At the start of a word μπ is a plain “b”. Inside a word most speakers say “mb”, some just “b”. Both are fine.

title: σ sounds “z” before β, γ, δ, λ, μ, ν, ρ
body: Before these soft, buzzing consonants σ buzzes too and becomes “z”. Most often you meet it in σμ.

title: τσ sounds “ts” as in “cats”
body: τσ is one sound, “ts” as in “cats”, and it can start a word or a syllable.

title: γγ sounds “ng-g” as in “finger”
body: γγ is not a double “gh” but “ng” plus a hard “g”, as in “finger” or “anger”. Exception: συγγνώμη (sorry) is “see-GHNO-mee”.

title: ; is the Greek question mark
body: Greek writes a question mark like an English semicolon (;). Read the sentence as a question, with the voice rising or falling as in English.

title: Two accents in one word: the second one is the main stress
body: When μου, σου, του, μας etc. follow a word stressed three syllables from the end, it gets a second accent on its last syllable. Stress both, the second more strongly.

title: ή, πού, πώς: the accent tells a word from its twin
body: One-syllable words carry no accent, except a few that would look like an unstressed twin: ή “or” vs η “the”, πού “where?” vs που “that, who”, πώς “how?” vs πως “that”. The marked one gets more weight.

title: γκ sounds “g” (often “ng” inside a word)
body: At the start of a word γκ is a hard “g” as in “go”. Inside a word it is usually “ng-g” as in “finger”, or just “g”.

title: Diaeresis (¨) or an accent on the first vowel splits a pair
body: Two dots (ϊ, ϋ) mean the vowel is said on its own: αϊ is “a-ee”, not “e”. An accent on the first letter does the same: τσάι is “TSA-ee”. ΐ carries both marks.

title: γχ sounds “nkh”, γξ sounds “nks”
body: Before χ and ξ, γ is an “n” said at the back of the mouth, as in “ink”: γχ is “n” plus the rough “kh”, γξ is “nks”.

title: The apostrophe (’) marks a dropped vowel
body: A vowel has been left out, and the word is said together with the next one: γι’ αυτό is one breath, “yaf-TO”.

title: τζ sounds “dz”
body: τζ is one sound, “dz” as in “adze”; in some loanwords it is closer to the “j” of “jam”. It is mostly found in borrowed words.
